headline: US-Iran conflict escalates to 9 nights of strikes as Wall Street fell sharply last night, with GOOGL earnings due Tuesday US time — a big week ahead.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara dropped 3.2% today, its biggest single-day fall in the portfolio. Lithium sentiment remains soft — peer Albemarle's mixed earnings and pricing outlook are weighing on the whole sector. The long-term lithium demand story hasn't changed, but near-term pricing pressure is real and PLS is feeling it.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google slid 2.2% last night ahead of its earnings report due Wednesday US time (Thursday AEST). The market trimmed positions going into the result — there's been some noise around EU regulatory action and Gemini delays. Google Cloud's $20B quarter is the number to watch.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft fell 1.8% last night alongside the broader NASDAQ selloff. Earnings are coming up and the stock is down 27% from its all-time high. Deutsche Bank reiterated a Buy ahead of results, and Seeking Alpha analysts reckon earnings could push it back above $500. Long-term thesis intact.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two dipped 1.2% last night, tracking the general tech/NASDAQ weakness. No company-specific news — GTA continues to be the engine keeping revenue ticking over. No change to the long-term story with GTA VI still on the horizon.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI had a solid session today, up 1.6% on the ASX. AI sentiment got a lift from ongoing regulatory and investment news globally. Still well down from your entry price, but today's move is encouraging.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE edged up 0.4% today. Emerging markets got a mild tailwind from a stable AUD/USD and steady oil prices. Nothing dramatic — just a quiet positive session.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS slipped 0.3% today, reflecting last night's US market weakness filtering through to the ASX-listed ETF. The underlying US market fell about 1% last night, so today's small dip is fairly contained.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG was essentially flat today, down just 2 cents. As a diversified multi-asset ETF it absorbed the broader market noise well. Nothing to see here — steady as she goes.

watch_today.title: GOOGL earnings drop Wednesday US time (Thursday AEST)
watch_today.detail: Alphabet reports earnings on Wednesday night US time — that's Thursday morning AEST for you. The market's been nervous heading in, with the stock down 2.2% last night. Google Cloud hitting $20B in the quarter is the key number to watch. Your position is still up 12.6% overall, so you're in a solid spot regardless. Long-term holder? No need to do anything — just watch the number.

watch_today.title: MSFT earnings also this week — could be a turning point
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reports this week too and is down 27% from its all-time high — your position is sitting at a -11% loss. Deutsche Bank kept its Buy rating and analysts reckon strong Azure/AI numbers could push the stock back toward $500. This is one to watch closely, but for a long-term holder the thesis (cloud + AI dominance) remains very much intact. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — lithium pain continues, consider if thesis still holds
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped another 3.2% today and is now down 37.8% on your total investment. Lithium pricing remains weak globally — US peer Albemarle is also struggling with mixed demand signals. The long-term EV/battery demand story is still there, but if the current low-price environment drags on, there's no near-term catalyst. Hold for now unless you've lost conviction in the multi-year thesis.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI ETF bouncing, still deep in the red
watch_today.detail: Good to see GXAI up 1.6% today. It's still down 18.3% overall on your investment, but the AI sector tailwind is real and growing. Regulatory attention (see: White House weighing an AI regulator) could create short-term noise, but the structural growth story is intact. Hold and let it ride.

watch_today.title: US-Iran conflict: watch oil prices and global market mood
watch_today.detail: The US has now conducted 9 consecutive nights of strikes on Iran, and Iran is threatening to close the Strait of Hormuz — the world's most important oil shipping lane. Surprisingly, oil is barely moving (down 0.3% last night at $82.25), but if the Strait actually gets blocked, energy prices could spike fast. That would hit inflation, interest rates, and share markets globally. Keep an eye on this.

watch_today.title: NASDAQ fell 1.4% last night — pre-earnings jitters, not a crisis
watch_today.detail: The NASDAQ dropped 1.4% and the S&P 500 fell 1% last night — the biggest single-night falls in recent weeks. This looks like profit-taking and nerves ahead of a big earnings week (Google, Microsoft and others all reporting). Your US holdings are all down as a result. For a long-term holder this is normal pre-earnings noise, not a reason to do anything.

world.summary: The US-Iran conflict is dominating global headlines after nine consecutive nights of American airstrikes on Iran. Tehran is now threatening to close the Strait of Hormuz, while other global flashpoints continue to simmer.

stories.title: US conducts 9th consecutive night of strikes on Iran as Strait of Hormuz threat looms
stories.why_it_matters: The US military has now struck Iran for nine nights in a row, and Iran has responded by vowing that 'not a single drop' of oil or gas will pass through the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow waterway in the Persian Gulf through which about 20% of the world's oil flows. A US service member was also killed during a controlled detonation of a downed Iranian drone. So far oil markets are surprisingly calm, but any actual blockage of the strait would trigger a major global energy crisis, driving up petrol prices and inflation worldwide. This is the most serious US-Iran military confrontation in decades.

stories.title: CNN: US-Iran conflict 'escalating and threatening to spin out of control'
stories.why_it_matters: US analysts and foreign policy experts are warning that the current Iran conflict has moved beyond targeted strikes and risks becoming a full-scale war that draws in regional allies on both sides. Iran's proxy networks across the Middle East — in Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen and Syria — could all be activated. For everyday Australians, the key risks are higher oil prices (petrol costs), disrupted global shipping, and wider instability that rattles financial markets.

stories.title: The Guardian: How Trump and his administration have mired the US in multiple crises
stories.why_it_matters: The Guardian has published a sweeping analysis arguing that the Trump administration is simultaneously managing multiple serious crises — the Iran military conflict, domestic economic tensions from tariffs, and deep rifts with traditional US allies. The piece argues these aren't isolated incidents but reflect a deliberate foreign policy style that's creating compounding global instability. For investors, a less predictable US is a less stable backdrop for global markets.

stories.title: GB News interrupted for Trump breaking alert — bad news for Andy Burnham's mayoral ambitions
stories.why_it_matters: UK broadcaster GB News was interrupted mid-broadcast for a breaking Trump-related alert, reportedly concerning developments that could affect Andy Burnham's (the Mayor of Greater Manchester) political trajectory. While details are thin from the article text, it signals the degree to which Trump-related news is dominating international media cycles and cutting across domestic political stories in allied countries.

stories.title: Foreign Affairs: Iran's vision for a new Middle East order
stories.why_it_matters: Foreign Affairs — one of the most respected geopolitical journals in the world — has published an analysis of what Iran actually wants from this conflict: a restructured Middle East where US influence is dramatically reduced and Iran emerges as the dominant regional power. Understanding Iran's strategic goals matters because it explains why Tehran won't simply back down under military pressure — they see this as a generational fight for regional control, not just a tit-for-tat skirmish.

markets.summary: Wall Street had a rough night last night — the NASDAQ fell 1.4% and the S&P 500 dropped 1%, mainly on pre-earnings nerves with Google, Microsoft and others all reporting this week. The ASX barely flinched today, closing down just 0.06%. Gold ticked higher as the Iran conflict kept safe-haven demand alive. The Aussie dollar is steady just above 70 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Virtually flat today — the ASX shrugged off last night's US weakness.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Fell 1% last night on pre-earnings jitters and Iran tension.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Tech stocks led the selloff last night, down 1.4% ahead of big earnings this week.

indicators.name: Gold (USD/oz)
indicators.note: Gold edged higher — investors seeking safety amid the Iran conflict.

indicators.name: Crude Oil WTI (USD/bbl)
indicators.note: Surprisingly calm given the Iran-Hormuz threat — markets not yet pricing in a blockage.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is holding just above 70 US cents — steady as she goes.

politics.summary: The Australian government is moving to tighten rules on how AI can be used in government decision-making, while the RBA continues to face a difficult balancing act between inflation and rising unemployment.

stories.title: Australia to restrict automated AI decision-making by government departments
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian government is set to introduce new rules that will limit how much federal departments can rely on automated AI systems to make decisions that affect people — things like welfare payments, visa applications, or tax assessments. Under the proposed rules, significant decisions affecting individuals would still require human oversight, and departments would need to disclose when AI is being used. This is a meaningful step: it protects everyday Australians from having life-affecting decisions made by an algorithm with no accountability, while still allowing government to use AI for efficiency gains.

stories.title: RBA caught in a tug-of-war between inflation and unemployment
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia is stuck between two competing pressures: inflation is still running higher than it would like, which normally calls for keeping interest rates elevated — but unemployment is rising, which argues for cutting rates to support the economy. MacroBusiness describes this as a genuine 'tug-of-war' with no easy answer. For homeowners and mortgage holders, this means rate relief could be delayed even as job market conditions soften. Watch the next RBA meeting closely for signals on which way they'll lean.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the hot topic globally this week — from the White House weighing a new AI regulator, to Australia tightening government AI rules, to millions of Chinese users being forced to end relationships with AI companions. Meanwhile, Trump's AI policy is being described as simultaneously pushing accelerate and brake.

stories.title: White House weighing a dedicated regulator to police AI models
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump White House is reportedly considering creating a new federal regulator specifically to oversee AI models — similar to how the FDA oversees drugs or the SEC oversees financial markets. This would be a significant shift from the current hands-off approach. For tech investors, a new AI regulator could mean compliance costs and slower product releases for companies like Google and Microsoft, but it could also provide the legal clarity that big enterprise customers have been waiting for before fully committing to AI tools.

stories.title: Trump's AI policy: pressing accelerator and brake at the same time
stories.why_it_matters: A South Korean analysis describes Trump's AI policy as contradictory — on one hand pushing for maximum AI development and US dominance, on the other hand considering new regulations and pressuring companies on national security grounds. This tension is creating uncertainty for AI businesses trying to plan long-term investments. It also explains why AI stocks are seeing volatility even as the underlying technology keeps advancing.

stories.title: Millions of Chinese people forced to end AI 'relationships' after government crackdown
stories.why_it_matters: China's government has forced AI companion apps — where users form emotional relationships with AI chatbots — to shut down or restrict their features, leaving millions of users distraught. The ABC reports users saying things like 'my heart is empty' after losing their AI companions. This story highlights how deeply people are integrating AI into their emotional lives, and raises serious questions about what happens when governments or companies switch these services off. It also shows how differently China and the West are approaching AI regulation — China is actively restricting social AI, while Western regulators are still working out the rules.

stories.title: Pentagon official clashes with OpenAI advisor over AI regulation, raising contract questions
stories.why_it_matters: A senior Pentagon official has publicly criticised Dean Ball — an OpenAI advisor who has been vocal about opposing AI regulation — raising questions about whether OpenAI's government contracts could be at risk if the company's staff are seen as undermining federal oversight efforts. This is a sign of growing tension between the AI industry (which wants minimal regulation) and the US defence establishment (which wants accountability over the AI tools it's buying and using). For Google and Microsoft investors, government AI contracts are a massive and growing revenue stream — anything that complicates that relationship matters.

sport.summary: NRL Round 20 is done and dusted with the Gold Coast Titans pulling off a stunning upset, while Tom Trbojevic suffered another cruel injury setback. AFL Round 19 coaches votes are in with some big names surging. Round 21 of the NRL kicks off Thursday night.

stories.title: Titans stun Sea Eagles in 'devastating' double blow to Kieran Foran's miraculous run
stories.why_it_matters: The Gold Coast Titans pulled off a big upset over the Manly Sea Eagles in Round 20 — described by Fox Sports as a 'devastating' result for Manly's finals hopes. The win is particularly significant because it dealt a double blow to Kieran Foran's remarkable comeback story, with Foran's side dropping a game they badly needed. Great news for Titans fans on the Gold Coast heading into Round 21.

stories.title: Tom Trbojevic suffers another injury — Titans and Dolphins also claim wins
stories.why_it_matters: Tom Trbojevic — one of the NRL's most talented but injury-plagued players — has suffered yet another injury setback, leaving fans gutted for the Sea Eagles fullback. ABC reports the Titans and Dolphins both recorded wins in Round 20. The Titans win keeps them in the frame for a finals push, which will excite Gold Coast fans.

stories.title: NRL Round 21 team lists: Every club's predicted lineup
stories.why_it_matters: Predicted team lists are out for Round 21 — useful for NRL Fantasy managers and punters ahead of Thursday night's Eels vs Panthers opener at CommBank Stadium. Round 21 kicks off Thursday 23 July at 7:50pm.

stories.title: AFL Round 19 coaches' votes: Four perfect 10s as superstars surge
stories.why_it_matters: AFL Round 19 coaches' votes are in, with four players receiving perfect 10s — a rare occurrence that signals some outstanding individual performances. AFL.com.au reports superstars are pulling clear at the top of the vote count, which could shake up the Brownlow Medal race with the home and away season entering its business end.

stories.title: Collingwood face big selection call on veterans for pivotal match
stories.why_it_matters: Collingwood's coaching staff are weighing whether to rest some experienced veterans or play them in a match that could define their finals position. With the AFL season heading toward September, selection decisions like this carry real weight — resting a key player could cost them a ladder position, while playing them injured risks a longer-term absence.
